'''''Nicotiana rustica''''', commonly known as '''Aztec tobacco'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=NIRU|taxon=Nicotiana rustica|accessdate=20 July 2015 }}</ref> or '''strong tobacco''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=17 October 2014 }}</ref> is a [[rainforest]] plant in the family [[Solanaceae]] native to South America. It is a very potent variety of [[tobacco]], containing up to nine times more [[nicotine]] than common species of ''[[Nicotiana]]'' such as ''[[Nicotiana tabacum]]'' (common tobacco).<ref name="Rapé study">{{cite journal |last1=Stanfill |first1=Stephen B. |last2=Oliveira da Silva |first2=André Luiz |last3=Lisko |first3=Joseph G. |last4=Lawler |first4=Tameka S. |last5=Kuklenyik |first5=Peter |last6=Tyx |first6=Robert E. |last7=Peuchen |first7=Elizabeth H. |last8=Richter |first8=Patricia |last9=Watson |first9=Clifford H. |title=Comprehensive chemical characterization of Rapé tobacco products: Nicotine, un-ionized nicotine, tobacco-specific N′-nitrosamines, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and flavor constituents |journal=Food and Chemical Toxicology |date=August 2015 |volume=82 |pages=50–58 |doi=10.1016/j.fct.2015.04.016 |pmid=25934468 |pmc=5704902 }}</ref> More specifically, ''N. rustica'' leaves have a nicotine content as high as 9%, whereas [[Nicotiana tabacum|''N. tabacum'']] leaves contain about 1 to 3%.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.3390/molecules27228105 |doi-access=free |title=Fractionation and Extraction Optimization of Potentially Valuable Compounds and Their Profiling in Six Varieties of Two Nicotiana Species |date=2022 |last1=Laszlo |first1=Csaba |last2=Kaminski |first2=Kacper |last3=Guan |first3=Haifeng |last4=Fatarova |first4=Maria |last5=Wei |first5=Jianbing |last6=Bergounioux |first6=Alexandre |last7=Schlage |first7=Walter K. |last8=Schorderet-Weber |first8=Sandra |last9=Guy |first9=Philippe A. | last10=Ivanov | first10=Nikolai V. |last11=Lamottke |first11=Kai |last12=Hoeng |first12=Julia |journal=Molecules |volume=27 |issue=22 |page=8105 |pmid=36432206 |pmc=9694777 }}</ref> The high [[concentration]] of nicotine in its leaves makes it useful for producing [[pesticide]]s,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.stanfordchem.com/scientists-found-nicotine-a-useful-pesticide.html |title=Is Nicotine A Useful Pesticide? |website=Stanford Chemicals |last=Higgins |first=Maria |date=4 November 2010 |access-date=22 September 2024 |archive-date=22 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240922175340/https://www.stanfordchem.com/scientists-found-nicotine-a-useful-pesticide.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and it has a wide variety of uses specific to cultures around the world. However, ''N. rustica'' is no longer cultivated in North America (except in small quantities by certain Native American tribes) as [[Nicotiana tabacum|''N. tabacum'']] has replaced it.<ref name="ley196512">{{Cite magazine |last=Ley |first=Willy |date=December 1965 |title=The Healthfull Aromatick Herbe |department=For Your Information |magazine=Galaxy Science Fiction |pages=88–98 }}</ref>

==Uses==
===South America===
[[File:Kupka tabaki (snuff).jpg|thumb|Rapé, a type of [[Snuff (tobacco)|snuff]] tobacco]]
''Nicotiana rustica'' is called ''mapacho'' in South America. It is often used for [[entheogen]]ic purposes by South American [[Shamanism|shamans]],<ref>{{cite book |date=1992 |title=Food of the Gods: The Search for the Original Tree of Knowledge - A Radical History of Plants, Drugs, and Human Evolution |publisher=Bantam |isbn=978-0-553-37130-7 |page=196 |chapter=Shamanic Tobaccos }}</ref> because of the comparatively high levels of [[harmala alkaloid]]s and [[nicotine]].<ref>{{cite journal |journal=Economic Botany |date=1976 |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=295–297 |title=Nicotiana an hallucinogen? |author=Oscar Janiger and Marlene Dobkin de Rios |doi=10.1007/bf02909739 |bibcode=1976EcBot..30..295J |s2cid=774652 }}</ref> There are many methods of administration in South American [[Ethnobotany|ethnobotanical]] preparations. In a preparation known as ''singado'' or ''singa'', ''N. rustica'' is allowed to soak or be infused in water, and the water is then [[insufflation (medicine)|insufflated]]. In Peru it is known as "Mapacho" and is smoked in pipes or drunk as a juice. The plant can also be smoked in [[cigar]]s, administered as an [[enema]], and made into a lickable product known as ''ambil''. Finally, ''N. rustica'' is a common ingredient in ''rapé'', a fine powder which is blown into the nostrils during ceremonies. ''Rapé'' is often a combination of ''N. rustica'' and a host of other herbs, depending on the intended use, including [[tonka bean]]s, [[cinnamon]], [[clove]] buds, [[sodium carbonate|soda ash]]<ref name="Rapé study" /> (creating ''[[nu-nu]]''), [[Anadenanthera]], [[Erythroxylum]], [[Virola]], and more.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilbert |first=J |date=1991 |title=Effects of Nicotine on Biological Systems |publisher=Birkhauser Verlag |page=11 |isbn=978-3-0348-7459-5 }}</ref> In Amazonian traditions, rapé is a finely powdered nasal snuff typically prepared from the leaves of ''Nicotiana rustica'' mixed with ashes derived from the bark of particular tree species.<ref name="Prue2018">{{Cite journal |last=Prue |first=Barbara |year=2018 |title=The healing power of tobacco: Smoking in the Peruvian Amazon |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=219 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2018.03.001 |pmid=29544895 }}</ref> The dried ingredients are pounded and filtered to produce a very fine dust.<ref name="Rennie2017">{{Cite journal |last=Rennie |first=Lucy |year=2017 |title=Characterization of Amazonian rapé tobacco snuff products purchased online |journal=Tobacco Regulatory Science |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=495–506 |doi=10.18001/TRS.3.4.7 |pmid=29911130 |pmc=5998811 }}</ref> Varieties of ''N. rustica'' used include “corda”, “moi”, and in some contexts fermented ''mapacho''.<ref name="Prue2018" /> Due to its high nicotine content—often several times greater than ''Nicotiana tabacum''—rapé is considered potent and is used ritually for its grounding and focusing effects.<ref name="Rennie2017" /> The choice of tree ashes and additional plant ingredients varies among different groups and is often specific to individual tribes.<ref name="Prue2018" />

===Russia===
In Russia, ''N. rustica'' is called ''makhorka'' (маxорка). Historically, makhorka was smoked mainly by the lower classes. ''N. rustica'' is a hardy plant and can be grown in most of Russia (as opposed to other ''Nicotiana'' species which require a warm climate), it was more readily and cheaply available, and did not depend on transport in a country with an underdeveloped road network and climatic portage problems. This remained the case until cultivated tobacco became widely available in the 20th century.

During [[History of the Soviet Union|Soviet times]], rustic tobacco was an important [[industrial crop]] of agriculture. In those times, dozens of varieties were bred, some of them considered equal in quality to [[cultivated tobacco]]. In modern times, makhorka is still sometimes smoked by peasants and farmers due to its high availability and being almost free for them.{{Cn|date=April 2024}}

===Vietnam===
{{original research|section|date=October 2023}}
[[File:Hút thuốc lào.jpg|thumb|200px|right|A man smoking thuốc lào with a bamboo pipe]]
The plant is called ''Thuốc lào'' in Vietnam, and is most commonly smoked after a meal on a full stomach to "aid in digestion", or along with [[green tea]] or local beer (most commonly the cheap [[bia hơi]]). A "rít" of thuốc lào is followed by a flood of [[nicotine]] to the [[Circulatory system|bloodstream]] inducing strong dizziness that lasts several seconds. Heavy cigarette smokers have had trouble with the intense volume of smoke and the high nicotine content; side effects include nausea and vomiting.{{cn|date=April 2025}}

There are many "brands" of tobacco, most of which are specific to the region in which they are grown. Some of these "brands" are mellow in flavor and effect, some are more energizing, and some are known for their relaxing properties.{{cn|date=April 2025}}

Water pipes can be found everywhere, and are a fixture of local tea booths, eateries, and cafes. It is common to find a table with a small box of tobacco at these establishments from which anyone can help themselves to a bowl during a tea or work break.{{cn|date=April 2025}}

The main difference between smoking thuốc lào and the use of other tobaccos is in the method of consumption, in that thuốc lào is consumed with a [[bong|water pipe]]. The smoker is presented with either a bamboo pipe called a ''điếu cày'' (English: "farmer's pipe") or a ceramic [[hookah]] called a ''điếu bát''. It may also occasionally be smoked in a more uncommon pipe known as a ''điếu ống''. The pipe is filled with an appropriate amount of water and a small amount of thuốc lào is pressed into the bowl.{{cn|date=April 2025}}

[[File:SacredTobacco.jpg|thumb|right|Flowering ''Nicotiana rustica'']]
[[File:Cánh đồng thuốc lào - Nicotiana rustica field.JPG|thumb|''Nicotiana rustica'' field in [[Quảng Xương]] district, [[Thanh Hóa province]], Vietnam ]]
One then ignites the tobacco and inhales to create a body of smoke inside the pipe, before exhaling the smoke, reversing the process of air in the pipe by blowing into it to pop out the tobacco. The smoker then sharply inhales, usually tilting the pipe upwards to an almost horizontal position (but not completely, as the water would drain into the mouth).

===Turkey===
''Maraş otu'' (English: Maraş weed) is a [[Chewing tobacco|chewing]] variant of ''Nicotiana rustica'' commonly used by people who live in [[Kahramanmaraş|Maraş]], Turkey and other areas of the country. Maraş Otu is a mixture of [[Oak tree]] ash and ''Nicotiana rustica'' that resembles [[henna]]. They use this by putting the mixture under their lips like Swedish ''[[snus]]'' or Afghan ''[[naswar]]''. It is recognized as a drug by anti-drug activists.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uyusturucu.info.tr/maras_otu.asp |title=Uyuşturucu |access-date=9 January 2016 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304102634/http://www.uyusturucu.info.tr/maras_otu.asp |url-status=live }}</ref> It can contribute to mouth cancers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Idris |first1=A.M. |last2=Prokopczyk |first2=B. |last3=Hoffmann |first3=D. |title=Toombak: A Major Risk Factor for Cancer of the Oral Cavity in Sudan |journal=Preventive Medicine |date=November 1994 |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=832–839 |doi=10.1006/pmed.1994.1141 |pmid=7855117 }}</ref>

===Sudan===
In Sudan, this type of tobacco is called toombak ({{langx|ar|توومباك}}). It has been used for over 400 years. Toombak being a form of [[smokeless tobacco]], the tobacco leaves are cured, dried, ground and then mixed with [[sodium bicarbonate]]. As such, the [[freebasing|freebase]] nicotine in this product is highly addictive.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Idris |first1=A. M |last2=Ibrahim |first2=S. O |last3=Vasstrand |first3=E. N |last4=Johannessen |first4=A. C |last5=Lillehaug |first5=J.
